Newborn Care

Pelvic-floor recovery after birth: eight things worth knowing

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pregnancy and birth can change how your pelvic floor feels and works. Leaking urine, pressure or discomfort may be common, but you do not have to accept them as the permanent price of having a baby. Recovery is individual, and useful treatment starts by identifying the problem. More squeezing is not always the answer: muscles need strength, coordination and the ability to relax.

What the pelvic floor does

The pelvic floor is a group of muscles and supporting tissues across the base of the pelvis. It extends between the pubic bone, tailbone and sides of the pelvis, helping support the bladder, uterus and bowel. The urethra, vagina and anus pass through this region.

These muscles help maintain bladder and bowel control and contribute to sexual function. They need to contract when support is required and relax to allow comfortable emptying. A muscle can be tense without working well, so pelvic health cannot be measured simply by how tightly someone can squeeze.

Pregnancy places extra demands on the pelvic floor. Vaginal birth may stretch muscles and nerves or involve a tear, an episiotomy or an assisted delivery. A cesarean birth avoids some vaginal injury but does not remove the effects of pregnancy, possible labour or abdominal surgery. Symptoms deserve attention after either type of birth.

1. Leakage is common, but it is a reason to ask for help

Urine may leak with coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting or a sudden urge to use the toilet. Early recovery can involve changes in muscle support, nerve function, swelling and bladder sensation. Leakage is not proof that a muscle has been permanently torn, and continuing symptoms are not limited to people with a recognised birth injury.

There is no single six-week deadline by which every bladder must recover, nor a dependable three-month rule for a particular grade of tear. Some people improve quickly; others need longer and benefit from treatment. The postnatal check is a useful opportunity to talk, but you do not need to wait for it if symptoms are troublesome.

Tell your midwife, primary-care clinician or pelvic-health physiotherapist when leakage occurs and how it affects daily life. Mention difficulty passing urine, incomplete emptying or reduced bladder sensation as well. Being unable to urinate needs prompt assessment rather than an exercise plan. Avoid solving leaks by severely restricting drinks, which can add to constipation and discomfort.

2. Weakness and excess tension can both happen

The idea that everyone becomes permanently loose after birth is misleading and can create unnecessary shame. Muscles may be weak, overactive, poorly coordinated or affected by a combination of these changes. You cannot tell which problem is present from the appearance of the vulva or from a partner’s opinion.

Pain, swelling, a healing tear or an episiotomy can make someone unconsciously brace the area. An episiotomy is a surgical cut, rather than a spontaneous tear. Muscle guarding may make relaxation difficult, including during a bowel movement, an examination or sex.

A tense pelvic floor can still lack strength or endurance. Repeated forceful contractions may increase symptoms when relaxation is the missing skill. A physiotherapist can assess how the muscles work and choose strengthening, relaxation or coordination work accordingly. Treatment should respond to your symptoms rather than pursue tightness as a goal.

3. Healing pain should be taken seriously

Some perineal soreness is expected after a tear, stitches or an episiotomy, and recovery can take weeks. The amount of pain and its course vary with the birth and the injury. A statement that all pain lasting more than a day is abnormal is too broad, but persistent or worsening pain should not be dismissed as inevitable.

Ask about pain relief suitable for you, including if you are breastfeeding. Keep the area clean according to your maternity team’s advice, change pads regularly and avoid irritating products. Comfortable positions and short periods of rest may help. A physiotherapist can contribute to recovery, but first a clinician may need to check wound healing, infection or another cause of pain.

Contact your maternity team promptly for increasing pain, fever, a wound that opens, pus or unpleasant-smelling discharge, or difficulty passing urine. Severe pain or feeling very unwell needs urgent care. Do not massage a painful or unhealed wound to try to release tight muscles.

4. Pelvic-floor exercises work best when they suit the problem

Pelvic-floor muscle training, often called Kegel exercises, can be helpful. It is not accurate to say that these exercises are always harmful or should never be used on their own. NICE recommends supervised training for at least three months as a first-line approach for stress or mixed urinary incontinence.

A useful programme is more than repeatedly clenching as hard as possible. It may develop gentle activation, strength, endurance, quicker responses and complete release between contractions. Your clinician can check technique, adjust the amount of practice and review progress. The three-month treatment period is not a reason to postpone the first assessment.

If exercises cause pain, increase pressure or make emptying harder, stop that exercise and ask for an assessment. People with excessive muscle tension may need relaxation and other treatment before or alongside strengthening. If a general online routine has not helped, that is a reason to reconsider the diagnosis and technique, not evidence that you failed.

Surgery is not the automatic next step when an unsupervised Kegel routine does not work. Other causes, physiotherapy options, bladder and bowel habits, and sometimes treatments such as a pessary may need discussion. The plan depends on what is actually causing the symptoms.

5. Comfortable intimacy does not follow a fixed calendar

There is no universal date when you should feel ready for sex. Healing, fatigue, mood, feeding demands and your own interest all matter. A six-week appointment does not create an obligation to resume penetration, and choosing closeness without penetration is a valid option.

Hormonal changes after birth, particularly while breastfeeding, can contribute to vaginal dryness. A suitable lubricant may help; choose a product compatible with any condoms you use. Scar discomfort, infection, pelvic-floor tension and other conditions can also cause pain, so lubrication is not a solution to every problem.

If penetration hurts, pause instead of pushing through it. Explain the discomfort to your clinician and ask whether wound healing, dryness or muscle function needs assessment. Persistent pain can need both medical and physiotherapy care. Internal massage, stretching tools or other techniques should not be started simply because an online article recommends them.

Sexual pleasure and orgasm depend on many physical and emotional factors. They cannot be predicted by how loose or tight the muscles feel. The aim of recovery is comfort, choice and function, rather than a promise to return to a particular sexual performance.

6. Notice pressure, bowel changes and other quieter symptoms

Not every pelvic-floor problem causes obvious leakage. You might feel heaviness, dragging, a bulge at the vaginal opening or a sensation of sitting on something. These can be signs of pelvic organ prolapse, although an examination is needed to understand what is happening. Symptoms can be worth treating even without a large visible bulge.

Mention dribbling after urination, trouble starting or finishing a urine stream, difficulty emptying the bladder, constipation, or trouble passing a bowel movement even when the stool is soft. Leaking wind or stool and being unable to defer a bowel movement also deserve attention, especially after a significant tear.

These symptoms are not all caused by weak muscles and are not diagnosed solely from a checklist. An infection, wound problem or another bladder or bowel condition may need to be considered. A history of when symptoms began and what makes them worse helps the clinician choose the right assessment.

You do not need to wait until symptoms are severe, until six weeks have passed or until they interfere with every activity. If you feel embarrassed, write them down and hand the list to the clinician. Asking specifically about urine, bowel control, pressure and pain can make it easier to discuss the whole picture.

7. You have a choice about an internal examination

A pelvic-health appointment usually begins with questions about symptoms, pregnancy and birth, earlier health problems, bladder and bowel habits, activity and your goals. A clinician may also look at breathing, posture, movement and abdominal recovery. You can explain what is most important to you, such as walking comfortably or reducing leaks.

An internal vaginal examination may be offered to assess muscle contraction, release, tenderness and healing. It is optional and requires your consent. You may decline, ask for another appointment, request a chaperone or ask the clinician to stop. Tell them about trauma, anxiety or pain so that care can be adapted.

When appropriate, an assessment may use a gloved, lubricated finger to feel muscle function. The clinician should explain what they propose and why; do not assume that every appointment uses the same technique. Other examinations or tests, including a rectal assessment for certain bowel problems, require their own explanation and agreement.

An internal examination is intimate and should not be described as noninvasive simply to make it sound less significant. If you do not want one, ask what can be learned through discussion and external assessment, and what uncertainty remains. Advice and parts of treatment can often begin without it.

Treatment may include education, breathing and relaxation, tailored muscle training, bowel and bladder advice, activity progression or selected hands-on techniques. Internal manual treatment is not compulsory, and no single technique guarantees recovery. Agree on goals and a review point rather than assuming that one appointment must resolve everything.

8. Prevention and access to care matter after every type of birth

Information about pelvic health belongs in routine pregnancy and postnatal care. Learning a comfortable contraction and release, discussing constipation and knowing which symptoms to report can help people seek support earlier. Cesarean recovery should not be treated as a reason to exclude pelvic-health questions.

Some birth circumstances, such as an assisted delivery or a more significant tear, may lead the maternity team to recommend closer follow-up or supervised training. NICE supports preventive pelvic-floor training during and after pregnancy, with additional supervised support considered for specific risk factors.

This does not mean that every person must buy a private internal assessment after birth. Routes to physiotherapy, referral criteria, appointment timing and insurance coverage vary. Ask your maternity service or primary-care clinician what is available and whether there is a self-referral option.

If you are told to wait but symptoms are worsening, ask what needs checking now and what should trigger an earlier review. A written plan can make the difference between supported recovery and being left to repeat exercises without knowing whether they are suitable.

A gentle starting point for practice and daily activity

After an uncomplicated birth, gentle movement and pelvic-floor practice can often begin when you feel able. Follow your own maternity advice after a significant tear, complication or operation. If you have a urinary catheter, wait until it is removed and you are passing urine normally before starting the exercises.

In a comfortable supported position, imagine gently closing around the back passage as if holding in wind, then lifting inward around the vagina and urethra. Keep breathing and avoid bearing down or strongly gripping the buttocks. Let the muscles fully soften again. A small comfortable contraction is more useful than a painful maximal effort.

Do not repeatedly stop your urine stream as a training exercise. The image of stopping urine can help identify the muscles, but practice should happen away from emptying the bladder. If you cannot feel a lift or release, or are unsure whether you are pushing downward, ask for technique guidance.

The number and length of contractions should suit your starting ability. Build gradually using the plan you are given, with rest between efforts. Pairing practice with a familiar daily moment can help, but missing a session during a demanding newborn day does not undo recovery.

Return to walking and other activity in manageable stages. Pain, increasing pressure or leakage during an activity are reasons to adjust it and seek advice. Keep stools comfortably soft, avoid straining, and ask about constipation treatment when needed. Recovery involves daily habits and rest as well as exercises.

When to seek urgent help

Get prompt maternity or medical advice if you cannot pass urine, cannot empty the bladder properly, have worsening perineal pain, fever, a wound problem or new loss of bowel control. These should not be left for a routine physiotherapy appointment.

Call emergency services for sudden heavy bleeding with faintness or a racing heart, chest pain, difficulty breathing or collapse. A very severe headache with visual changes after birth also needs urgent assessment. These may be unrelated to the pelvic floor but are important postpartum warning signs.

For less urgent symptoms, arrange a review and record what is happening: leaks with particular movements, pain location, pressure, bowel changes and whether symptoms improve or worsen over the day. The purpose is to guide treatment, not to grade how successfully you have recovered.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pelvic-floor training is supported for prevention and for conditions such as stress or mixed urinary incontinence. The programme should account for muscle strength, coordination, relaxation and symptoms.

Persistent leakage, pressure or pain deserves assessment. An internal examination may help but is optional, and treatment should respect consent and individual recovery.

How BeMama can help

At the next postnatal conversation, name one symptom you most want help with and one activity you want to return to comfortably. Ask for a specific next step and review date.

When to seek help

Urinary retention, worsening pain with fever or wound changes, heavy bleeding with faintness, and chest or breathing symptoms require prompt or emergency medical care.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Common postpartum symptoms are still worth discussing and treating.
  • The pelvic floor needs to relax as well as contract; more squeezing is not always better.
  • An internal assessment is optional and requires your consent.
  • Seek help according to symptoms rather than waiting for a fixed recovery deadline.

Frequently asked questions

Is leaking urine normal after birth?

It is common, but you do not have to accept it indefinitely. Tell your clinician when it happens and whether it is improving. Assessment and an appropriate exercise plan can help, and you do not need to wait for a routine check if it is troubling you.

Can my pelvic floor be tight and weak at the same time?

Yes. Muscle tension does not necessarily mean useful strength or coordination. Difficulty relaxing can coexist with leakage or poor endurance, so an individual assessment is more helpful than assuming everyone needs stronger contractions.

Should everyone do more Kegels?

No. Pelvic-floor training is useful for many people, but the technique and amount must suit the problem. Exercises that increase pain, pressure or emptying difficulty should be reviewed rather than intensified.

When can I begin gentle exercises?

Often when you feel able after an uncomplicated birth, following your maternity advice. Wait until a urinary catheter is removed and you are passing urine normally. Complications, significant injury or pain may require a tailored plan.

Should I stop my urine halfway through to practise?

No. Repeatedly interrupting urine flow is not recommended training. Use the idea to recognise the muscles, then practise contraction and full release away from the toilet.

Do I need an internal examination to get help?

No. It may provide useful information, but you can decline, request a chaperone or ask for it to stop. Ask what can be assessed externally and whether a later examination would change the plan.

Why can sex hurt even after stitches have healed?

Dryness, scar sensitivity, muscle tension and other conditions can contribute. Pause painful penetration and seek advice rather than pushing through. A lubricant may help dryness but does not replace assessment of persistent pain.

Do I need pelvic-floor care after a cesarean?

Pelvic-health information and symptom assessment are relevant after a cesarean too. Pregnancy and any labour affect the body, and abdominal surgery has its own recovery needs. Treatment depends on your symptoms and circumstances.

Does a heavy or bulging feeling mean severe prolapse?

Not necessarily. Pressure or a bulge can have different causes and levels of severity. A clinician can assess it and discuss options; symptoms need not become severe before you ask for help.

When should I seek help before my postnatal check?

Do so for troublesome or worsening symptoms. Inability to urinate, fever with worsening wound pain, a wound opening or new bowel-control problems need prompt assessment. Heavy bleeding with faintness or chest and breathing symptoms require emergency help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
